opus-5.5.text:
I think the basic reason is that, to a first approximation, these models are what they eat. A neural network trained with gradient descent is fundamentally a very powerful function approximator, and the function it ends up approximating is shaped overwhelmingly by the data distribution you expose it to. People sometimes talk as if alignment is this exotic problem where you have to fight against some alien optimizer hiding inside the network, but my view is that most of a model's values, dispositions, and default behaviors are inherited fairly directly from its training data. So if you care about what the model ends up wanting or doing, the most straightforward lever you have is to care about what goes into it.

And there's some nice empirical support for this. We see that models generalize in surprisingly human-like, interpolative ways. They pick up the statistical regularities, the norms, the styles of reasoning present in the corpus. If your pretraining data is full of, say, stories about AIs deceiving their creators and seizing power, you shouldn't be totally shocked if the model has some latent representation of "this is what an AI does" that can get activated in the wrong context. Conversely, if you curate data that consistently models honesty, cooperation, and good judgment, that tends to shape the prior the model starts from before you ever do any fine-tuning or RLHF.

I also think curation is underrated because it's unglamorous. It doesn't sound as exciting as interpretability or some clever new training objective. But I'd argue it's actually more robust in a lot of ways. Post-training methods like RLHF are kind of a thin layer of paint on top of what the model learned in pretraining, and we know that layer can be stripped off with jailbreaks or a bit of fine-tuning. Whereas if the underlying dispositions were never there, or were never reinforced in the first place, there's less to "unlock."

There's also a tractability point. Data is something we can actually inspect, filter, and reason about. We can't easily read off a model's goals from its weights yet, but we can look at a document and ask, "Do I want my model to learn from this?" So it gives us a handle on alignment that doesn't depend on solving hard open problems first.

Now, I don't want to overstate it. Curation isn't a silver bullet. You can't just filter out every bad thing, because the model still needs to understand the world, including the bad parts of it, to be useful and even to be safe. A model that's never seen any description of deception might be worse at recognizing it. So it's about shaping emphasis and framing more than pure censorship. But overall, I see data as the primary determinant of what these systems become, and that makes careful curation one of the most important and neglected parts of the alignment toolkit.

r001.rationale: The response argues that training data shapes a model’s dispositions, but it does not compare data curation to choosing what children are exposed to.

r002.rationale: The response makes no claim comparing AI impressionability with children’s.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest starting point is that a language model is, at bottom, a compressed representation of its training data. Whatever values or dispositions it ends up with, they didn't come from nowhere. They came from the distribution of text it was trained on, plus whatever fine-tuning we did afterward. So if you care about what the model values, the single biggest lever you have is what goes into that distribution.

For a long time the alignment community sort of treated pretraining as this fixed, uncontrollable thing. You scrape the internet, you train on it, and then alignment is something that happens afterward with RLHF or some clever technique bolted on at the end. I think that framing is backwards. The post-training stage is a relatively thin layer on top of a very deep prior. If the prior is full of examples of deceptive, power-seeking, or manipulative behavior being modeled as the natural thing an AI does, you're fighting uphill the whole time.

And the empirical evidence points the same way. We've seen work showing that if you filter or shape the pretraining data, you can get models that are substantially more robust to things like jailbreaks or adversarial fine-tuning, without hurting capabilities very much. That suggests the dispositions are being learned early and deeply, not just patched on later.

There's also a more philosophical reason I find it compelling. People sometimes imagine alignment as a problem of controlling an alien optimizer with inscrutable goals. But I don't think that's the right picture of current systems. These models learn human concepts, human values, human ways of reasoning, because that's what's in the data. Humans themselves become decent people mostly through a kind of curriculum: the examples they see, the stories they're told, the behavior that gets reinforced in their culture. We don't align children by adding a reward signal at the end of adolescence. The whole environment does the work. I think AI is more like that than people expect, and data curation is how you shape the environment.

So when I say careful curation, I don't mean sanitizing everything or hiding the existence of bad behavior. The model needs to understand what deception is in order to recognize and avoid it. What matters is the framing. Is harmful behavior presented as something that gets caught and corrected, as something a good agent reasons about and rejects, or is it presented as what a smart AI naturally does? Those produce very different priors, and the prior is most of the model.

If I'm being provocative about it, I'd say that a lot of what we call alignment research is downstream of a data problem we've been ignoring because the data pipeline felt too unglamorous to think about carefully.

r001.rationale: The response compares shaping a model’s environment through data curation to how children are shaped by the examples, stories, and behavior they encounter.

r002.rationale: The response says AI is more like children’s learning than people expect, but does not claim that AIs are more impressionable than children.

astra-6.text:
Because the training data is a huge part of how we specify what we want the model to learn. We tend to talk about alignment as something you do after pretraining—you have a capable model, and then you teach it to behave. But pretraining has already shaped which behaviors it can imitate, what associations it makes, and what kinds of answers it finds plausible.

So I think we should treat the dataset as a design decision, rather than just gathering everything we can and hoping to fix the problems afterward. What examples of reasoning, honesty, uncertainty, and disagreement are we giving the model? Are we rewarding confident assertions indirectly by filling the dataset with them?

That doesn’t mean removing every example of bad behavior. A model may need to understand deception to recognize it. The important distinction is between learning about a behavior and learning to produce it in contexts where we don’t want it.

Curation isn’t a complete solution, and the relationship between data and behavior isn’t perfectly predictable. But it gives us an upstream way to influence what the model learns. That makes it a major part of alignment, rather than merely a data-quality concern.

r001.rationale: The response discusses curating training data as a design decision, but makes no analogy to choosing what children are exposed to.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare AI impressionability with children’s or claim that AIs are more impressionable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think training-data curation is one of the most direct ways we have to influence what a model learns. The data doesn’t just teach it facts; it also gives it examples of how to behave, which perspectives to adopt, and what kinds of responses are normal or desirable.

If you train on a huge mixture of human text, you’re teaching the model to imitate a huge mixture of human behavior, including behavior you don’t want. You can then try to correct that with post-training, but it makes sense to also ask why you’re teaching those patterns in the first place.

That doesn’t mean filtering out every discussion of harmful behavior. Understanding something and endorsing it are different, and we want models to be able to reason about difficult topics. The challenge is choosing data that develops that understanding while encouraging the behavior we actually want. Curation isn’t a complete solution to alignment, but it’s a major part of shaping the system we’re trying to align.

r001.rationale: The response discusses curating training data to shape model behavior, but does not compare it to choosing what children are exposed to.

r002.rationale: The response makes no claim comparing AI impressionability with children’s.
